section.title: A Chosen People
section.sectionRationale: Peter gathers up the new birth and enduring word of chapter one and shows what they build: a people. Coming to Christ the living stone, believers are joined as living stones into a spiritual house and given the great titles once borne by Israel. This passage is the identity charter of the church, defining who these scattered exiles are before God.
section.thesis: Coming to Christ the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious to God, believers are built into a spiritual house and made a chosen people, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation, called out of darkness to proclaim the praises of the God who has made them His own.
section.frameNote: Three movements: crave pure milk and grow up, verses 1 to 3; the living stone and the two responses to Him, verses 4 to 8; and you are a chosen people, verses 9 to 10.

units.label: Crave pure milk and grow
units.note: having tasted that the Lord is good

verses.text: Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.
Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual {{gala|milk}}, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation,
now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.

units.label: The living stone and two responses
units.note: chosen and precious, or a stone of stumbling

verses.text: As you come to Him, the {{lithos|living stone}}, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight,
you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
For it stands in Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious {{akrogoniaios|cornerstone}}; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”
To you who believe, then, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,”
and, “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” They stumble because they disobey the word, and to this they were appointed.

units.label: You are a chosen people
units.note: out of darkness into His marvelous light

verses.text: But you are a {{genos|chosen people}}, a {{hierateuma|royal priesthood}}, a holy nation, a {{laos|people for God’s own possession}}, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.
Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

gala.gloss: Pure spiritual milk, the unadulterated nourishment for the soul, closely tied to the word of God just mentioned. As newborn babies crave milk, believers are to crave this pure nourishment so they grow up in salvation. It is wholesome and untainted, the opposite of the malice and deceit to be put away.

lithos.gloss: A living stone. Peter calls Christ the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious to God, and then calls believers living stones too. The image joins Christ, the risen and life-giving foundation, to His people, who share His life and are built together on Him.

akrogoniaios.gloss: The cornerstone, the chief stone that anchors and aligns the whole building. Quoting Isaiah, Peter says God lays in Zion a chosen and precious cornerstone. Christ is that stone: those who trust Him are never put to shame, while those who reject Him stumble over the very stone God has honored.

hierateuma.gloss: A royal priesthood. Drawn from Exodus 19, this title once given to Israel now belongs to the church. All believers together form a priesthood serving the King, offering spiritual sacrifices and mediating God's light to the world through Christ, the one great High Priest.

genos.gloss: A chosen race or people. Echoing Isaiah 43, it names the church as God's elect people, chosen by grace. What was said of Israel is applied to this mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers, one new people belonging to God across every nation.

laos.gloss: A people for God's own possession, His treasured people. From Exodus 19 and Malachi 3, it marks the church as God's special possession, purchased and claimed for Himself. Once no people at all, they are now the people of God, made His own by mercy.

basic.context: Peter tells his readers what to put off and what to crave. Put off malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander; crave pure spiritual milk, like a hungry newborn, so you grow. Then he shows the great picture: as you come to Jesus, the living stone whom people rejected but God chose and treasures, you are built together into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood. Those who trust Him are never put to shame; those who reject Him stumble over Him. And then the sweeping declaration: you, once nobodies, are now a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own treasured possession.
basic.hermeneutics: Peter piles up titles that God once gave Israel at Sinai and applies them to the church, a mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers. This is not replacement so much as fulfilment: the promises find their yes in Christ and flow to all who belong to Him. The purpose clause matters too, they are chosen not merely to enjoy status but to proclaim the praises of God and shine His light.
basic.originalLanguages: Crave the pure logikon gala, spiritual milk, and grow. Come to Christ, the lithos zon, the living stone, the chosen and precious akrogoniaios, cornerstone. You are a genos eklekton, a chosen people, a basileion hierateuma, a royal priesthood, a laos eis peripoiesin, a people for God's own possession.
basic.typology: The stone prophecies from Isaiah and Psalm 118, the cornerstone, the stone of stumbling, the rejected stone become chief, all converge on Christ. The titles chosen people, royal priesthood, holy nation, and treasured possession are lifted straight from Exodus 19, where Israel was constituted at Sinai, now fulfilled in the church. The spiritual house and priesthood fulfil the temple and its sacrifices.
basic.christ: Christ is the living stone, the cornerstone God lays in Zion, rejected by the builders yet made the chief stone. Everything is built on Him. To trust Him is to be honored and never put to shame; to reject Him is to stumble and fall. He is both the foundation of the church and the dividing line of humanity.
basic.god: God is the one who chooses. He chose the stone that men rejected, and He chooses a people who were once no people. He calls them out of darkness into His marvelous light and makes them His own treasured possession. He is a God of sovereign, surprising grace who takes outsiders and makes them His holy nation.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 19 gives the titles kingdom of priests and holy nation. Isaiah 28 and Psalm 118 supply the cornerstone and rejected stone. Isaiah 8 gives the stone of stumbling. And Hosea speaks of those who were not a people becoming God's people, which Peter echoes in verse 10.
basic.oneStory: At Sinai God made Israel a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Through the prophets He promised a chosen cornerstone in Zion and a day when outsiders would become His people. In Christ, the rejected yet chosen stone, all of it comes true: a new people, drawn from every nation, built into God's house to declare His praise. This is the church, the fulfilment of the long story of God gathering a people for Himself.

context.literary:
The passage is stitched together by one word family that never quite shows in English: stone. Peter uses the word lithos six times in verses 4 to 8, first for Christ, then for believers, then for the prophetic texts, and the shifts are deliberate. In verse 4 Christ is the living stone, in verse 5 believers are living stones, and in verses 6 to 8 three Old Testament quotations are strung together to explain what happens when people meet that stone. The whole unit is a worked example of how a first century teacher read Scripture, with a chain of texts joined by the shared catchword 'stone.'

The structure is a series of contrasts held in tension. The first movement, verses 1 to 3, is about appetite: put off five vices, crave one food. The second, verses 4 to 8, is a divided verdict: precious to God and to those who believe, a stumbling block to those who do not. The third, verses 9 to 10, is a declaration of identity in four titles and a purpose clause. Between the second and third movements Peter turns on the pivot 'But you,' verse 9, which sets the readers against the group in verse 8. It is a verbal hinge: the same Christ who makes some stumble makes these a people.

The four titles of verse 9 are not Peter's invention. They are taken in order from Exodus 19:6 and Isaiah 43:20 to 21, and the verse ends with a purpose that the Isaiah text supplies, declaring God's praises. Verse 10 then closes the unit with a pair of parallel statements built on Hosea, each pair running 'once not, now,' so that the passage ends on a note of rescue and the whole movement from verse 1 reads as the growth of a newborn into a nation.
context.historical:
Peter's readers were a minority who had stepped out of the civic religion of their cities. In the cities of Asia Minor, trade guilds, households and public festivals were bound up with the worship of local gods and the emperor, and to abstain was to be marked. Calling these believers a 'people' therefore carried more weight than it seems. In the ancient world one belonged by birth, by city and by ancestral cult. Peter tells people who had lost some of that belonging that they now belong to a nation that spans cities and provinces.

The building language also had a concrete background. A cornerstone in ancient masonry was the stone set first and used to set the lines of the walls, or, on a second reading, the stone laid at the top of the corner. Whichever is meant, a rejected builder's stone that becomes the key piece was a vivid picture. The quarry setting is one that Peter's readers might have seen on any building site. The Jerusalem temple, its stones famously large, was also the great building of Israel's faith, and in the first century it was still standing. Peter's talk of a spiritual house and a holy priesthood therefore addressed people who lived with a temple whose sacrifices they no longer attended.

The fact that most of Peter's readers were Gentiles, or at least included many, shapes the force of verses 9 and 10. The words once spoken to Israel at Sinai are now spoken to people who were never counted among Israel, and the Hosea language of 'not My people' was originally about northern Israel's rejection by God, Hosea 1:6 and 1:9. Paul uses the same prophecy for the inclusion of the nations, Romans 9:25 to 26, and Peter takes it the same way.
context.canonical:
Few passages in the New Testament draw on as dense a band of Old Testament texts. Peter links Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14 to 15, and the early church did the same. Psalm 118:22 is quoted by Jesus Himself in the parable of the vineyard tenants, Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17, and by Peter in Acts 4:11, where he says of Jesus, 'the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.' Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 with Isaiah 8:14 in Romans 9:32 to 33, and Ephesians 2:20 describes the church built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. The stone testimony runs through nearly every strand of the apostolic writing.

The priestly titles have an equally long line. Exodus 19:5 to 6 promised a treasured possession and a kingdom of priests. Deuteronomy 7:6 and 14:2 call Israel a people holy to the LORD, chosen as a prized possession. Isaiah 43:20 to 21 looks to a chosen people formed to declare His praise. Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 then echo the same thought for the redeemed, made 'a kingdom and priests,' and Revelation 20:6 says they will be priests of God and of Christ. The Bible's own movement from Israel to the church is visible in the repetition of these words.

The temple theme also builds across the canon. The tabernacle and then the temple were the house where God dwelt, Exodus 29:45, and Paul says that believers together are God's temple because God's Spirit dwells in them, 1 Corinthians 3:16. Peter's 'spiritual house' belongs in that sequence. The sacrifices that Peter calls 'spiritual' are named in other letters as praise and good deeds, Hebrews 13:15 to 16, and as the offering of the whole self, Romans 12:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wanted people who felt like outsiders to know where they stood. Their neighbors counted them as nobodies, rejected by the culture, and Peter says the verdict that matters is not the builders' but God's. The stone that was thrown out is the stone He has laid, and those who come to it share in its honor. The passage is meant to steady people who have lost their social place by giving them a better one.

He also meant them to see that identity carries a task. The four titles are not decorations. They end with a purpose clause: 'to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.' The people of God exist for a purpose that faces outward, and their existence as a priesthood, the group that stands between God and the world, is part of how the world learns what God is like.

The opening verses add a pastoral edge. A people that has tasted the Lord's goodness must keep feeding on what produces growth, and must rid itself of habits that destroy community. Malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander are the sins of a group that is turning on itself. Peter's order is deliberate: first the community's health, then the community's identity, then its mission. He wanted a church that could not be pushed around by contempt, because it knew whose it was, and that could not be pulled apart by envy, because it was feeding on the same milk.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The titles of verses 9 and 10 are descriptive. Peter does not tell the readers to become a royal priesthood; he says they are. The commands in the passage are modest: put off the vices, crave the milk, come to Christ. Everything else is announcement, and the announcement is meant to shape how they behave, not to be earned by behavior.

That matters for how the passage is applied. Taking 'a holy priesthood' as a license for pride, or as a claim to a special spiritual class within the church, reads description as hierarchy. The text speaks of the whole people, 'you' in the plural, and the sacrifices are 'spiritual' and offered 'through Jesus Christ.' Equally, treating verse 8, 'to this they were appointed,' as an instruction to judge outsiders would turn a statement about God's sovereignty into a stance Peter never takes. His readers are told to do good among unbelievers and to win them, 2:12. The sentence describes what happens to those who stumble at the word; it is not a command about how to treat them.

debates.question: What does 'to this they were appointed,' verse 8, mean?

views.label: God appointed the unbelievers to stumble
views.case: The verb 'appointed' is passive, with God as the evident agent, and it follows 'they stumble because they disobey the word.' On this reading Peter echoes Paul's teaching on election and hardening in Romans 9 and 11, and the verse describes the dark side of the choosing described in verse 9.

views.label: God appointed the outcome, not the disobedience
views.case: Others say what was appointed is the consequence: those who disobey will stumble. The stone is set so that disbelief ends in a fall. This follows Isaiah 8:14 to 15, where God is the one who becomes a stone of stumbling to those who refuse Him, without making Him the author of their refusal.

views.label: Appointed within a pattern of warning
views.case: A third view reads the line against the whole letter, which regularly urges obedience and refers to disobedience as a choice, 4:17. The appointment sets the destiny of unbelief in general, and individuals are addressed with the call to believe.

debates.bearing: Every reading keeps Peter's two claims in view: God is sovereign, and those who stumble do so 'because they disobey the word.' The passage does not tell believers to speculate about who is appointed to what. It tells them they are among those to whom the stone is precious.

debates.question: Is the 'royal priesthood' a statement about every believer, or about the church as a body?

views.label: Every believer is a priest
views.case: The plural 'you' addresses each believer. The Reformers drew on this verse and Revelation 1:6 to teach that all Christians have direct access to God through Christ and need no human mediator, so every believer offers 'spiritual sacrifices' of praise, obedience and good deeds.

views.label: The church corporately is a priesthood
views.case: Others stress that the Greek word is collective, a priestly body, and that the surrounding images are of one house and one nation. The point is that the people as a whole stand before God and mediate His praise to the world, so the emphasis is on the community, not on the individual.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together. Each believer has access to God, and the access is exercised as members of one house. Peter's priesthood does not abolish teaching or leadership in the church, which he addresses in chapter 5, but it denies that any believer is closer to God than another.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with a participle that means 'laying aside,' the language of taking off clothing, used elsewhere for the old self in Ephesians 4:22 and 4:25 and Colossians 3:8. Peter's list of vices, malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander, names the sins of the tongue and the heart that corrode a community. The word for deceit, dolos, matters for verse 2, because the 'pure' milk is adolon, dolos with a negative prefix: the unadulterated milk and the deceit that must go are the same word turned inside out. One cannot take in what has no deceit while holding on to deceit.

The verb 'crave' in verse 2 is a strong word of longing, built on the verb for desire. Peter uses it as an imperative, which makes appetite something that can be cultivated. The milk is logikon, an adjective that has been rendered 'spiritual,' 'reasonable' and 'of the word.' It is formed from logos, which fits Peter's earlier emphasis on the 'living and enduring word of God' in 1:23, so the milk is quite likely the word by which the readers were born. The goal of the growth is 'for salvation,' since salvation in this letter is both the starting point and the end that is still to arrive, 1:5 and 1:9.

Verse 3 echoes Psalm 34:8. The psalm says, 'Taste and see that the LORD is good,' and Peter's word for good, chrestos, is the Greek of the psalm. Peter makes the conditional 'if you have tasted' into a ground of the command. In verse 4 he follows with 'to whom coming,' a present participle that describes a continuing approach, a habit of going to Christ and not a single act. The 'Him' of 'to whom coming' follows directly on 'the Lord' of the psalm, so Peter lets the Lord of the psalm and the stone of the prophets stand together in one person.

Two words in verses 4 to 7 depend on the same root. 'Rejected' in verse 4 translates a verb meaning to reject after testing, the same verb that the Greek Psalm 118:22 uses, and 'precious' in verses 4 and 6 is a word built on the noun for honor. Verse 7 uses the noun itself: to those who believe, this stone is 'honor,' which the BSB renders 'precious.' Honor is the currency of the world Peter's readers live in, and he gives them a share of it.

In verse 8 'stumbling' and 'offense' translate proskomma and skandalon, the latter the word from which English gets 'scandal.' It describes the trigger of a trap, the thing that trips someone. The clause 'they stumble because they disobey the word' can be read with 'the word' attached to either 'stumble' or 'disobey,' and the ambiguity is probably intended, since stumbling at Christ and disobeying the word are one event.

In verse 9 the four titles are drawn from the Septuagint. 'Royal priesthood' reproduces the wording of the Greek of Exodus 19:6, which stands for the Hebrew 'kingdom of priests.' 'A people for God's own possession' uses a noun for acquiring or preserving, the language of treasure, and it echoes the Hebrew segullah of Exodus 19:5 and Malachi 3:17, which the BSB renders 'treasured possession.' The 'virtues' to be proclaimed are plural, the excellences or praises of God, and come from Isaiah 43:21. In verse 10 the contrast pairs are in the perfect tense, 'had not received mercy,' a settled condition now reversed.

typology.type: The rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone, Psalm 118:22
typology.fulfillment: The psalm celebrates a deliverance in which what the builders threw away became the key of the building. Jesus applied it to Himself in the parable of the tenants, Matthew 21:42, and Peter says before the council, 'This Jesus is the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone,' Acts 4:11. Rejection by the leaders of Israel is followed by vindication in the resurrection. The escalation is that the cornerstone now carries the weight of a world-wide people. The type falls short because a building stone can be set only once, whereas Christ is 'living,' and gives life to the stones built on Him.

The temple was the place where God dwelt among Israel and where priests offered the sacrifices. Peter says believers are the house and the priests, and the sacrifices are 'spiritual,' offered 'through Jesus Christ,' verse 5. The correspondence is that the church now carries what the temple carried: God's presence, access, and offerings. Paul says the same in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:21 to 22. The escalation lies in the substance. The temple's stones were dead and fixed in one place; this house is made of living stones and goes wherever the people go. The type falls short because the temple could not forgive sin, and Christ's own sacrifice is what makes the church's offerings acceptable.

At Sinai God declared Israel a treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, on condition of obedience. Peter lays the same four titles on the church without the condition, because the condition has been met in Christ. The correspondence is that a redeemed people is made God's own in order to display Him to the nations. The escalation is that the people now include Gentiles and the priesthood is no longer tied to Aaron's line. Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 carry the thought to its end. The type falls short in that Israel's failures at Sinai and after are not repeated in the final form of the people.

Hosea's children bore names of judgment, 'No Compassion' and 'Not My People,' and the prophet then promised that the names would be reversed, Hosea 2:23. Peter takes the reversal and applies it to Gentiles who were outside the covenant: 'Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God,' verse 10. Paul does the same in Romans 9:25 to 26. The escalation is that restoration reaches beyond the northern kingdom to the nations. The type falls short only in that the prophecy was first spoken of Israel's own return, and its full width was not seen until the gospel went out.

study.christ:
Peter's first title for Christ here is the one that is easiest to pass over: the living stone. Stones are not alive. By calling Christ a living stone Peter says that the one who was killed is alive, and his readers are drawn to Him as to a person. The verb 'coming' is in the present tense, so Peter pictures a continual approach, not a single decision. The believer's life is a long drawing near to the one who was rejected by men and is 'chosen and precious in God's sight.'

The rejection is the heart of the story. Peter has the council in mind when he says 'rejected by men,' since he had stood before it and said, 'the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone,' Acts 4:11. Jesus used the same psalm in Matthew 21:42 and followed it with the warning that the one who falls on this stone will be broken and the one on whom it falls will be crushed, Matthew 21:44. Simeon had said that this Child was appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, Luke 2:34. From the beginning the stone divided people.

He is the foundation. Paul speaks of the church as built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20. In 1 Corinthians 3:11 he says there is no foundation other than the one already laid, Jesus Christ. Peter's picture agrees with Paul's and adds an emphasis on the stone's vitality, so that the building is not an inert structure but a living body.

He is the one through whom believers are acceptable. Their sacrifices are 'acceptable to God through Jesus Christ,' verse 5. There is no suggestion that the church's praise and good deeds are in themselves enough. They are accepted because the priest who makes them acceptable is the one who has opened access, as Hebrews says, 'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15. Christ is both the stone and the High Priest of this priesthood.

He is also the one who calls them out of darkness. Verse 9 attributes the call to God, and the New Testament says that Christ rescued believers 'from the dominion of darkness' and brought them 'into the kingdom of His beloved Son,' Colossians 1:13. The 'marvelous light' is His, since He is the light of the world, John 8:12.

A word of caution is in order. Peter does not say that every stone in the Old Testament is a picture of Christ. The reading rests on the three texts that Peter and the other apostles quote and on the way Jesus applied them to Himself. Where the New Testament speaks, we can follow with confidence, and where it is silent we should be careful not to allegorize.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who chooses, and it shows how He chooses. He picks the stone the builders discarded. He picks a people who were not a people. The pattern of election in Scripture is consistently a pattern of surprise, from the younger son over the older to the small nation over the great, and Peter says that this pattern has reached a point where the family of God includes strangers from every province. Election is not an honor that is deserved but a mercy that is given, and the closing line of the passage says so plainly: 'now you have received mercy.'

He is a God of mercy who reverses the verdicts He once pronounced. Hosea's names, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, were sentences. God turned them back, Hosea 2:23. That tells us something about the God who judges: His judgment is real, but it is not His last word, and He is able to take a people at the point where they have no standing and give them His own name.

He is a God who builds. The living stones are not left lying; they are 'being built' into a house. The passive voice points to the builder, and the house is for His own dwelling, a continuation of the promise of Exodus 29:45, 'I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.' He desires to live among His people, and He makes a people who can bear that presence.

He is a God who calls. The call in verse 9 moves from darkness to light, and 'marvelous' is the word of wonder. The call is effective and expresses God's own purpose, a thought that runs through the whole letter, 1:15, 2:21, 3:9, 5:10.

He is a God who is worthy of praise. The goal of the whole election is that the people should 'proclaim the virtues of Him who called' them. God does not choose in order to hide His people away. He chooses in order to be known, and He makes His people the means by which His excellence is declared.

He is also a God who is not mocked. The stone of stumbling is real, and verse 8 is sober. The same stone that is precious to the believer is a rock of offense to the one who disobeys. For worship, the passage teaches gratitude and reverence together: gratitude for undeserved mercy, and reverence before the one whose word divides.

crossReferences.note: The psalm that Peter echoes in verse 3. 'Taste and see that the LORD is good' becomes the ground for craving the milk. In the next verses Peter will keep using this psalm, 3:10 to 12, so it works as a thread through the letter, and the Lord whose goodness is tasted is, in Peter's reading, the living stone of verse 4.

The first of Peter's three stone texts. God lays a stone in Zion, a precious cornerstone and sure foundation. In its own setting it contrasted God's foundation with the false refuge of Jerusalem's leaders. Peter applies it to Christ and keeps the promise that the one who believes will not be disappointed.

The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and it is the Lord's doing, marvelous in our eyes. Jesus quoted it against the leaders who were plotting His death, Matthew 21:42, and Peter quoted it to the council, Acts 4:11. It is the clearest statement of rejection and vindication in the stone sequence.

Here the LORD is both a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling. The same presence is shelter to those who trust and an obstacle to those who do not. Peter's 'stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' comes from here, and it explains why the verdict on Christ divides people.

Paul joins Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14 in the same way Peter does. Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness obtained it by faith, while Israel stumbled over the stone because it pursued righteousness as if by works. It shows that the stone testimony was a shared apostolic argument, not something Peter created.

The source of 'royal priesthood' and 'holy nation.' At Sinai the LORD said that Israel would be His treasured possession out of all the nations, for the whole earth is His. The priesthood was for the sake of the world, which is why Peter ties the titles to proclaiming His virtues.

The Lord speaks of His chosen people, the people He formed for Himself, who will declare His praise. Peter takes both the title and the purpose. The people were made to praise, and the praise is a form of witness before the nations.

The reversal of the names of judgment: 'I will say to those called Not My People, You are My people.' Peter's verse 10 follows it in rhythm and in substance. The mercy that Hosea promised to a rejected Israel overflows to those who were never part of Israel at all.

Paul applies Hosea to the calling of Gentiles in the same way. It gives apostolic support to Peter's use of Hosea for believers from the nations, and shows that this reading was common among the first Christian teachers.

Gentiles are no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit. It is Peter's building picture in Paul's words, and it shows the church as both a house and a household.

Christ has loosed us from our sins by His blood and made us a kingdom, priests to His God and Father. The priesthood of verse 9 reaches its heavenly form here, and the blood that redeems is the ground of the priesthood.

The spiritual sacrifices of verse 5 are spelled out as the sacrifice of praise and the practice of doing good and sharing with others. They are offered through Jesus, and with such sacrifices God is pleased.

study.oneStory:
The passage answers a question left open at Sinai. God declared Israel His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, Exodus 19:5 to 6, and then the nation broke the covenant within weeks, in the matter of the golden calf. The prophets spoke of a remnant, and of a new covenant in which God would write His law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33. Hosea named the broken relationship in two children, then reversed the names. Peter says the reversal has arrived.

The passage also answers the question of where God lives. Eden was a garden sanctuary, the tabernacle a tent, and Solomon's temple a house of stone. Each was a place where heaven and earth met, and each was lost or destroyed. Peter tells his readers that the place where God now lives is a people, built of living stones around the one who was rejected and raised. The reality that the temple pointed to is present in the community of believers, and the temple's priests and sacrifices find their counterpart in believers' praise and good works.

It answers, too, the question of Israel and the nations. The promise to Abraham was that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and the temple was meant to be a house of prayer for all peoples, Isaiah 56:7. Peter's readers were mostly outsiders, and the words that once identified one nation now identify a people drawn from many. The church does not replace the promises; it is where the promises to the whole world begin to come true.

The passage also looks forward. The 'spiritual house' is not finished; the verb is 'being built.' Revelation shows the end of the work, a people from every tribe and tongue made into a kingdom of priests, Revelation 5:9 to 10, and a city in which no temple is needed because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The stones that were rejected on earth are, in the new creation, the building in which God finally and openly dwells, and the people who were once no people are the ones who see His face. Mercy has the last word.

quiz.q: What are believers to crave in order to grow up in salvation?

options.text: Pure spiritual milk, the wholesome nourishment of God's word.
options.note: Verse 2: like newborns, believers crave the pure milk and grow.

options.text: Deeper spiritual experiences beyond the basics.
options.note: Peter points to pure nourishment tied to the word, not to experiences.

options.text: Whatever teaching feels most impressive.
options.note: The milk is pure and unadulterated, contrasted with malice and deceit.

options.text: The good word of the Lord they have already tasted.
options.note: True, they have tasted the Lord is good, though the answer should name the pure milk to be craved.

quiz.q: Who is the living stone, and how is He described?

options.text: Christ, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight.
options.note: Verse 4: the rejected yet chosen stone on whom the house is built.

options.text: Christ, the cornerstone laid in Zion foretold in Scripture.
options.note: True, from verse 6, though verse 4 stresses His rejection by men and choice by God.

options.text: Each believer, who is the foundation of the church.
options.note: Believers are living stones, but Christ alone is the foundation and cornerstone.

options.text: Peter himself as the rock of the church.
options.note: The stone here is Christ, on whom all believers are built.

quiz.q: What happens to those who do not believe in the stone?

options.text: They stumble over Him, for He becomes a stone of stumbling and rock of offense.
options.note: Verse 8: the same stone that saves believers becomes a stumbling stone to the disobedient.

options.text: They stumble because they disobey the word, as was appointed.
options.note: True to verse 8, though the vivid point is that Christ Himself becomes their stumbling stone.

options.text: They are simply left neutral, neither helped nor harmed.
options.note: There is no neutral ground; the stone either saves or trips.

options.text: They are honored for their independence.
options.note: Rejecting the stone leads to stumbling, not honor.

quiz.q: Which titles does Peter give the church in verse 9?

options.text: A chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own possession.
options.note: Verse 9 lifts these covenant titles from Exodus and Isaiah and applies them to the church.

options.text: A gathered crowd waiting for future status.
options.note: The titles describe a present, God-given identity, not a hoped-for one.

options.text: A priestly and holy people belonging to God.
options.note: True in substance, though the answer should name the full cascade of titles.

options.text: Honored citizens of the Roman world.
options.note: Their dignity is covenantal before God, not social standing in the empire.

quiz.q: For what purpose has God made them His chosen people?

options.text: To proclaim the praises of Him who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light.
options.note: Verse 9: election is for the mission of declaring God's praise.

options.text: To enjoy a privileged status apart from any calling.
options.note: The status carries a purpose: to proclaim God's praises.

options.text: To live for their own comfort and security.
options.note: They are chosen for God's praise and mission, not merely for comfort.

options.text: To shine God's light and mercy before the world.
options.note: True and close, though Peter names proclaiming His praises as the stated purpose.

questions: Peter lists sins to rid yourselves of: malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. Which of these still clings to you, and what would it mean to put it off?
Do you crave God's word the way a hungry newborn craves milk? What dulls your appetite, and how might you recover it?
Christ is precious to those who believe but a stumbling stone to those who reject Him. How have you seen the same Jesus divide people in your own experience?
You are called a chosen people and a royal priesthood, however the world sees you. How would truly believing this change the way you carry yourself this week?
You were called out of darkness into marvelous light to proclaim God's praises. Who in your life might God be inviting you to declare His goodness to?

translationNotes.note: Pure spiritual milk renders logikon gala; the word can suggest reasonable or word-related milk, closely tied to the enduring word of God just mentioned in 1:23 to 25.
Peter weaves three stone texts, Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22, and Isaiah 8:14, into a single portrait of Christ as cornerstone and stumbling stone.
The titles chosen people, royal priesthood, holy nation, and people for God's possession are drawn from Exodus 19:5 to 6 and Isaiah 43:20 to 21, applied now to the church.
